MANILA, Philippines – Artificial intelligence will change the direction of the labor-driven model of the Philippines, but how its changes will impact the country will depend on how companies respond to and invest in AI.

Boston Consulting Group collaborated with the Makati Business Club to release The Philippine AI Maturity Report last Wednesday, November 11. The report paints a picture of the Philippines as wanting to adopt AI to have a competitive advantage, even as the country deals with being about two years behind the global AI maturity curve.
While Philippine companies hold big ambitions for AI — with more than half aiming to reach the highest level of maturity by 2029 — gaps in talent, data, and execution continue holding back potential.

The report noted how Philippine labor cost is 70% below the Asia-Pacific average and 80% below the global average. The problem, however, is if demand for this labor will continue to be maintained in an age where some Philippine labor tasks are being offloaded to AI.

Said the report, “Many of the leading AI-native players emerged only after 2022, yet some have already reached significant scale with relatively small teams. As these technologies mature, firms in high-cost markets gain both a more viable alternative to offshoring routine work and a model for delivering services with fewer people.”

The report envisions two possible scenarios for the Philippines: either AI automates the work on which the Philippines currently competes for, eroding the traditional cost advantage, or AI augments the workforce and allows the Philippines to compete on capability rather than cost alone.

Currently, the report noted we are closer to the former scenario rather than the latter. It is suggested that, in light of the two possible scenarios, “Philippine firms have to overinvest in AI to become competitive in the regional landscape.”

The Philippines is playing catch-up to the global trajectory of AI use and adoption, with the country’s 2026 average maturity remaining closer to the global average from 2024 than to the global average today.
The report explained that “AI maturity is advancing quickly, and the benefits are increasingly accruing to companies that can move from experimentation to scaled, enterprise-wide adoption.”

Companies in the Philippines are thus working on embracing and adapting to AI at a rapid pace, with companies having three-year targets aiming for an average maturity increase of roughly 34 percentage points, or about 11 points per year. This is around 2.5x the actual pace of improvement recently observed in the global average.
As such, Philippine companies are ambitiously setting sights on what the report termed as “a major step-change in AI maturity” by 2029.
To that end, the report cites the weakest link that needs to be addressed: the people factor.

The report noted a gap between the building of AI capabilities versus how well AI capabilities are embedded into a given organization. The ways in which people work will help determine if AI is used properly and creates value for organizations.

“The next phase of AI maturity for the Philippines will therefore depend less on adding more foundations and more on activating them across people, processes, and ways of working so that existing AI capabilities translate into tangible business outcomes,” the report said.
The report also said Philippine companies invest in line with peers in IT and IT-based AI, but said that “greater value lies in non-IT AI to support business transformation, not just cost reduction.”
The report also emphasized three bottlenecks the Philippines has to deal with as it seeks to better get a handle on AI:

items: When it comes to data, companies lacking the integrated and usable data foundation needed to scale AI.
When it comes to talent, the country’s talent system does not yet consistently produce and retain the advanced skills AI requires.
When it comes to cost, Philippine companies face a tougher economic equation: they pay close to global prices for AI while operating against a lower local cost base.

blocks.text: Accordingly, the report concludes that if we want to take higher-value path in adopting and thriving in the AI-enabled future, we will need government and business to move and work together “to address the structural barriers to AI adoption while building the organizational capabilities needed to turn AI into sustained business value.”

To do this, the report suggests the government should address the bottlenecks by connecting fragmented data and digitizing Philippine business activity for AI, by building talent and providing Philippine talent convincing reasons to stay, and creating conditions to make AI affordable in the Philippines.
Meanwhile, it also recommended businesses do the following:

items: Set a focused, multiyear AI agenda with clear business outcomes
Pick a few strategic outcomes and win them
Focus on upskilling and transforming your people
Continue investing in the technology and data foundation
Be conscious of your tokens’ return on investment
Set up a tracking mechanism for AI impact but leave room for experimentation
